headline: US-Iran tensions spike oil prices and rattle Wall Street last night, while PLS.AX takes the biggest hit in today's ASX session — and the NRL Roosters snatch a 1-point Grand Final thriller.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara dropped 4% today to $2.64 — its worst single-session move in the portfolio. No specific news catalyst, but lithium sentiment remains deeply depressed as oversupply concerns persist globally. The stock is now down over 60% from your entry price. The long-term thesis (EV battery demand) is still intact, but recovery will take patience — this is a sector-wide problem, not a Pilbara-specific one.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: The AI ETF fell 2.79% today to $16.01, tracking weakness in US tech stocks from last night's NASDAQ sell-off. Both Google and Microsoft reported earnings that disappointed the market, weighing on AI-exposed stocks broadly. Down 15% from your entry, but the long-term AI growth story hasn't changed.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two slipped 1.67% last night to $190.17. The broader NASDAQ sell-off dragged it down alongside other tech names. Eyes are on November — earnings are due and the GTA VI release timeline continues to be the key question hanging over the stock.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft fell 1.55% last night to $521.91 after Q3 earnings drew a mixed reaction. Revenue and cloud growth were solid but the market had priced in perfection — investors sold on the news. Still up nearly 18% from your entry, so the long-term story remains very much intact.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google dropped 1.45% last night to $278.22 after Q3 earnings disappointed on search monetisation. There's debate about whether Gemini AI is cannibalising its own ad revenue. Some analysts still see it as a buy below $300. Down about 9.5% from your entry, but the long-term AI and search dominance case hasn't fundamentally broken.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE slid 1.16% today to $87.60, pressured by broader risk-off sentiment globally and ongoing concerns about the US-Iran conflict's impact on emerging market economies. Down 7.4% from entry, but emerging markets exposure remains a valid long-term diversifier.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS fell 0.69% today to $533.32, reflecting last night's weakness on Wall Street following Big Tech earnings disappointments. Still up 3.4% overall — a steady long-term US market holding.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG edged down just 0.25% today to $75.86, showing its diversification doing its job — global weakness was muted here. Slightly underwater overall (-1.8%) but well within normal range for a diversified growth fund.

movers.name: DHHF ETF
movers.note: DHHF barely moved today, down just 0.22% to $41.41. Essentially flat on your entry price (-0.5%). Nothing to act on here — this is exactly the kind of steady, boring behaviour you want from a core diversified holding.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Hold through the pain
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals dropped another 4% today to $2.64, and is now down a brutal 60%+ from your entry. But this is a sector-wide lithium price collapse, not a Pilbara-specific implosion. The company still has solid assets and balance sheet. Selling now locks in the loss — the only scenario to reconsider is if you fundamentally no longer believe in the EV transition. For a long-term holder, sit tight.

watch_today.title: GOOG: Earnings dip, but below $300 looks attractive
watch_today.detail: Google fell after Q3 earnings disappointed on search revenue, and analysts are debating whether Gemini AI is eating into ad income. However, multiple analysts still rate it a buy below $300 — and it's sitting at $278. For a long-term holder, this could be a moment to top up if you have spare cash. Nothing broken in the fundamental business.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Hold — earnings were solid, market just wanted more
watch_today.detail: Microsoft fell 1.55% last night despite decent Q3 numbers. Cloud (Azure) growth was strong, but the stock was priced for perfection and gave back some gains. You're still up ~18% overall. Long-term case — AI integration, cloud dominance — is unchanged. No reason to move.

watch_today.title: TTWO: Earnings due in November — watch closely
watch_today.detail: Take-Two has earnings coming this month, and the GTA VI release timeline is the single biggest variable for the stock. If Rockstar confirms a 2027 release window, expect a rally. If there's another delay, expect pain. You're down ~12% overall — hold and see what November brings before making any moves.

watch_today.title: Oil spiking on US-Iran tension — watch your cost of living and broader markets
watch_today.detail: Crude oil jumped over 2% last night to $104/barrel as the US-Iran conflict intensifies, with an LNG carrier hit in the Gulf and Iran threatening to expand the war. Higher oil means higher petrol prices and inflation pressure globally — which could flow through to RBA rate decisions and equity markets. Nothing to act on today, but this is worth watching closely this week.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: Hold — AI narrative intact even if prices wobble
watch_today.detail: The Global X AI ETF dropped 2.79% today following US tech weakness overnight. You're down 15% from entry, but the AI sector's long-term growth trajectory hasn't changed — if anything, the Google/Microsoft earnings underline how central AI is to both companies' futures. Hold and let time do the work.

world.summary: The US midterm elections tomorrow are dominating global headlines, with violence fears at polling booths, court orders against the Trump administration, and growing tensions with Iran — which is now threatening to expand its conflict beyond the Middle East.

stories.title: US election officials brace for violence and intimidation at polling booths
stories.why_it_matters: With US midterm elections falling tomorrow, election officials across the country are on high alert for voter intimidation and violence at polling booths. A federal judge has also ordered the Trump administration to stop threatening election officials with prosecution — suggesting a serious escalation of political pressure on the people who run the voting system. How the midterms go will directly shape US economic and foreign policy for the next two years, which flows through to global markets including Australia.

stories.title: How Trump and his allies are seeking to interfere in the US midterm elections
stories.why_it_matters: The Guardian is reporting that Trump and his political allies are actively working to influence the outcome of the midterms through a range of tactics. This comes alongside the court order blocking threats to election officials. The outcome of tomorrow's vote will determine whether Trump's Republicans hold or expand their grip on Congress — a result that could significantly affect US trade policy, tariffs, and aid to allies like Australia.

stories.title: Qatar LNG carrier hit by unidentified objects in the Gulf
stories.why_it_matters: A Qatari LNG (liquefied natural gas) ship — the Al Mayeda — was struck by unidentified objects while passing through the Gulf, in what appears to be another escalation tied to the broader US-Iran conflict. Qatar is one of the world's biggest LNG exporters, and Australia competes in the same market. Any disruption to Gulf shipping lanes pushes energy prices higher globally, and is already contributing to the oil price spike seen last night.

stories.title: Iran threatens war beyond the Middle East as US weighs new strikes
stories.why_it_matters: Iran is now openly threatening to expand its conflict beyond the Middle East if the US launches new strikes. Qatari mediators are holding a third day of talks trying to de-escalate the situation. This is a significant flashpoint — an expanded conflict would mean higher oil prices (already at $104/barrel), potential disruption to global shipping, and broader market volatility. Australia imports oil and exports LNG, so both sides of the trade are affected.

stories.title: What would another US-Iran conflict actually look like?
stories.why_it_matters: The Financial Times has run a military briefing outlining what a full US-Iran conflict could look like — covering Iranian missile and drone capabilities, US carrier groups in the region, and the risk of the Strait of Hormuz being closed. About 20% of the world's oil passes through that strait. A closure, even temporary, would send energy prices to levels not seen since 2008 and could tip major economies toward recession.

markets.summary: Last night was rough on Wall Street — the NASDAQ dropped nearly 3% and the S&P 500 fell 1.8%, dragged down by mixed Big Tech earnings from Google and Microsoft and rising fears around the US-Iran conflict pushing oil higher. Gold fell sharply. The ASX 200 held up well today, edging up 0.18% to close around 8,908 — a resilient result given the offshore headwinds. The Aussie dollar is essentially flat at 70.35 US cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Closed slightly higher today despite overnight Wall Street weakness — a solid defensive showing.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Fell 1.82% last night on mixed Big Tech earnings and rising geopolitical risk from the US-Iran conflict.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Down nearly 3% last night — worst performer among the indices, hurt hardest by Google and Microsoft earnings reactions.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil jumped over 2% on escalating US-Iran tensions and the LNG tanker attack in the Gulf.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold fell sharply by 3.3% — an unusual move that may reflect investors selling gold to cover losses elsewhere.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar was essentially flat, holding just above 70 US cents.

politics.summary: Australian political debate this weekend has centred on government spending, interest rates, and a mining policy reversal — with Gina Rinehart taking aim at Canberra as the RBA rate pain continues to bite.

stories.title: Government spends $3m+ on branded merch — including condoms and lollies
stories.why_it_matters: ABC News has revealed the federal government spent more than $3 million on branded merchandise — including condoms and lollies — in a finding that's giving opposition politicians fresh ammunition on the 'wasteful spending' front. It's politically embarrassing timing given the ongoing debate about whether the government is spending too much and adding to inflation pressure.

stories.title: Rinehart slams government spending as mining profits slide
stories.why_it_matters: Mining billionaire Gina Rinehart has publicly attacked the federal government over its spending levels, as her own mining operations face a profit slide. Rinehart argues high government spending is driving inflation and keeping interest rates elevated, directly hurting businesses and households. The comments add pressure on Labor ahead of what's shaping up as a big week of economic debate.

stories.title: Government rules out appeal on McPhillamys gold mine decision
stories.why_it_matters: The federal government has decided not to appeal a Federal Court ruling that overturned its ban on the McPhillamys gold mine in NSW. The original ban was controversial — Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek had blocked the mine on cultural heritage grounds, but the court struck it down. By not appealing, the government is effectively allowing the mine project to proceed, a significant backdown that will be watched closely by the mining sector.

stories.title: Banks hoarding billions in interest from savers as rates rise
stories.why_it_matters: ABC is reporting that Australian banks are sitting on billions in interest earnings that haven't been fully passed on to savings account holders, even as the RBA has lifted rates significantly. This is a classic squeeze — mortgage holders pay more, but deposit holders don't get the full benefit. It's likely to fuel calls for a parliamentary inquiry into bank profitability and fairness.

stories.title: Is the government really on an 'out-of-control' spending splurge? It's complicated
stories.why_it_matters: The Guardian has done a fact-check on the claim that the Albanese government is on an 'out-of-control' spending splurge — a key attack line from the opposition. The conclusion: it's more nuanced than either side claims. Spending is up in areas like defence, NDIS, and cost-of-living relief, but as a share of GDP it's not dramatically out of historical norms. Useful context for cutting through the political noise.

ai.summary: The big AI story this weekend is Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft all agreeing on a unified 'opt-out' standard for web scraping — meaning website owners can now block all major AI crawlers with a single setting. Meanwhile, Google has quietly launched Gemini 4 Carbon, a specialised AI model built to find and fix software security flaws.

stories.title: Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft agree on unified AI scraping opt-out
stories.why_it_matters: For the first time, all four major AI companies have agreed on a single standard that lets website owners block AI bots from scraping their content with one command, rather than having to block each company separately. This is a big deal for publishers, news organisations, and anyone who owns a website — it gives content creators more control over whether their work is used to train AI models. It's a sign the industry is trying to self-regulate before governments step in.

stories.title: What is Gemini 4 Carbon — Google's AI model for finding security flaws?
stories.why_it_matters: Google has launched Gemini 4 Carbon, a specialised AI model designed specifically to scan software code for security vulnerabilities and then suggest fixes. Unlike general-purpose AI, this model is trained to understand the nuances of cybersecurity threats. For businesses and developers, this could dramatically speed up the process of finding bugs before hackers do — think of it as an always-on security auditor that never sleeps.

stories.title: OpenAI vs Anthropic vs Google: The race for enterprise customers
stories.why_it_matters: A new analysis breaks down how OpenAI (ChatGPT), Anthropic (Claude), and Google (Gemini) are each trying to win over big business clients. OpenAI is leaning on brand recognition and plugin ecosystems; Anthropic is pitching safety and reliability for regulated industries like law and finance; Google is bundling Gemini into its existing Workspace tools that millions of companies already use. The winner of this race stands to generate enormous recurring revenue — directly relevant to your GOOG and GXAI.AX holdings.

stories.title: Gemini 3.1 Pro pricing breakdown vs Claude and GPT
stories.why_it_matters: Google's Gemini 3.1 Pro is now priced at $2 per million input tokens and $12 per million output tokens — making it significantly cheaper than comparable Claude and GPT-4 models. For developers and businesses building AI-powered apps, cheaper API costs mean faster adoption of Gemini. This is Google's strategy to gain market share: undercut the competition on price and use its cloud infrastructure advantage to scale profitably.

sport.summary: The NRL Rugby League World Cup is delivering drama — the Jillaroos made history with a massive win, there's controversy over a wildcard finish, and November 1 has triggered the NRL's annual off-season player signing frenzy. On the domestic front, the ASX 200 Grand Final was won by the Roosters over the Knights 19-18 in a heart-stopper.

stories.title: Roosters beat Knights 19-18 in NRL Grand Final thriller
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters won the 2026 NRL Grand Final 19-18 over the Newcastle Knights in one of the tightest finishes in recent memory — just one point the difference at fulltime at Accor Stadium. An absolute nail-biter for fans of both clubs.

stories.title: Jillaroos score historic World Cup 'massacre' — Isabelle Kelly hauls six tries
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian Jillaroos put on a World Cup masterclass today, running in a historic scoreline described as a 'massacre.' Star winger Isabelle Kelly was the standout, bagging an incredible six tries in the one match. The win cements Australia's status as the dominant force in the women's international game heading into the semi-finals.

stories.title: 'Never seen anything like this': Wild scenes after 'gobsmacking' RLWC finish
stories.why_it_matters: A RLWC group stage match produced one of the most chaotic finishes in World Cup history, with Fox Sports reporting scenes of disbelief from players, officials and fans alike. The French coach gave a furious media response after the result, suggesting a controversial call went against his team. The finish is already reshaping the semi-final qualification picture.

stories.title: NRL's November 1 signing war: 120+ off-contract stars up for grabs
stories.why_it_matters: November 1 is the NRL's annual 'transfer deadline day' equivalent — the date when players who are off-contract can officially be approached and signed by rival clubs. More than 120 players are available this year, making it one of the biggest off-season pools in years. Clubs are reportedly using secretive tactics to charm targets, and this will reshape several rosters heading into 2027.

stories.title: AFLW: Club misses finals by 0.2% in agonising ladder heartbreak
stories.why_it_matters: One AFLW club has been cruelly eliminated from finals contention by just 0.2% on the ladder — the smallest possible margin. The heartbreak comes down to percentage (the ratio of points scored versus points conceded across the season), meaning a single score in a single game earlier in the year cost them a finals berth. Fox Sports reports the result has created a ripple effect through the finals bracket.
